blocks.text: In Turkmenistan the everyday drink is tea, and above all green tea, *gök çaý*. As across Central Asia, it is drunk at all hours of the day. *Gök* usually means **blue**; for tea, and for fresh green plants, it means **green**.
The word *çaý*, like English **chai**, goes back to the Chinese word for tea, cha. In Turkmen it can mean more than the drink: a meal, often breakfast, or a visit spent sitting over tea.

Tea is brewed in a teapot, a *çäýnek*, and poured into a *käse*, a small bowl without a handle. Travel guides to the region describe a custom shared across Central Asia: the host fills each bowl only part of the way and tops it up again and again, so the tea stays hot and the guest is looked after. A bowl filled to the brim can hint that the visit should end.

At home, tea and meals are served on a cloth spread on the floor or on a low table, the *saçak*, with bread, *çörek*, on it. Families and guests sit around it together, and the teapot keeps going round.

The *çaýhana*, or teahouse, is the public version of this: a place to sit, drink tea, eat and talk, often for hours. The word joins *çaý* with *hana*, a Persian word for **house** or **room** that Turkmen also uses in *aşhana* (kitchen), *kitaphana* (library) and *hassahana* (hospital). In 2006 the food writer Darra Goldstein described one teahouse on the edge of Ashgabat set up as a row of camel-hair yurts.

blocks.title: Tea talk
blocks.text: With the present tense of this unit, tea talk is easy: *Çaý içýärin* (I'm drinking tea), *Çaý isleýärsiňizmi?* (would you like some tea?), *Biz her gün gök çaý içýäris* (we drink green tea every day). One tea, please, is *Bir çaý, haýyş edýärin*.
With the words of this unit, you can read this:

blocks.tk: Biz her gün gök çaý içýäris. Şu gün myhman gelýär. Çaý gyzgyn, käse kiçi. Biz çaý içýäris we gürleýäris.
blocks.en: We drink green tea every day. Today a guest is coming. The tea is hot, the bowl is small. We drink tea and talk.

vocab.en: tea; a meal, a visit over tea

questions.explain: *gök* is **blue**, but for tea and fresh plants it means **green**.

questions.q: What do *aşhana*, *kitaphana* and *çaýhana* have in common?
Why does a host pour only a little tea at a time?
options: To keep it hot and refill it often
To show the guest should leave
questions.explain: A part-filled bowl that keeps being refilled is a sign of care; a full one can hint at the end of a visit.

sources.title: Turkmen cuisine
